Solution 1 (conditional probabilities of reaching 4)[edit]

We will solve this using the law of total probability (otherwise apparently known in Olympiad folklore as the method of "states", presumably reflecting the fact that these are kids who won't yet have studied formal/axiomatic probability theory). Firstly, we note that the probabilities of the frog taking each of its possible moves always depend only on its current position, and not on how it got there - in other words, the frog, just like coins or dice, 'has no memory'. Therefore, we can unambiguously define as the probability of reaching given that the frog is currently at position . We want to find (since the frog starts at ), and of course .


For each value of , we now consider the conditional probabilities of reaching given that the frog takes each of the possible moves from its current position.
